sq.ANSWER:
A stack is a linear data structure that follows the LIFO (Last In, First Out) principle. When implemented using an array, elements are stored in a contiguous block of memory.

Advantages:

  1. Fast Access: Since an array is index-based, accessing stack elements is quick.
  2. Easy Implementation: Arrays are simple to use and require less programming overhead.
  3. Memory Efficiency (for small stacks): If the maximum size is known, arrays minimize memory fragmentation.

Disadvantages:

  1. Fixed Size: The stack size is determined at compile-time, leading to Stack Overflow if exceeded.
  2. Memory Wastage: If the stack is underutilized, allocated memory goes unused.
  3. Resizing Issues: If resizing is required, a new larger array must be allocated, and elements must be copied, which is inefficient.

Applications:

  1. Function Call Management: Stack is used to manage function calls and recursion in programming.
  2. Expression Evaluation: Used in postfix, prefix, and infix expression calculations.
  3. Undo/Redo Operations: Text editors and graphic software use stacks to store previous states.
  4. Backtracking Algorithms: Used in solving mazes, Depth-First Search (DFS), and puzzle solving.
  5. Memory Management: Stack memory is used in system processes to store local variables and return addresses.

sq.ANSWER:
A stack is a linear data structure that follows the LIFO (Last In, First Out) principle. It can be implemented using either arrays or linked lists, each having its own advantages and limitations.

Key Differences Between Linked List-Based Stack and Array-Based Stack

Feature

Array-Based Stack

Linked List-Based Stack

Memory Allocation

Uses static memory allocation, requiring a fixed size at declaration.

Uses dynamic memory allocation, growing or shrinking as needed.

Size Limitation

The size is predefined and cannot be changed at runtime, leading to Stack Overflow if exceeded.

No fixed size; the stack grows dynamically until memory is exhausted.

Memory Usage

Can result in memory wastage if the allocated array size is larger than the actual data required.

Uses only required memory, preventing wastage.

Performance (Access Speed)

Faster since elements are stored contiguously in memory and accessed using an index.

Slower because elements are stored non-contiguously, requiring pointer traversal.

Insertion and Deletion Complexity

Push (O(1)) if no resizing is needed, but resizing causes O(n) complexity. Pop (O(1)).

Push (O(1)) and Pop (O(1)) without resizing, as elements are linked dynamically.

Implementation Complexity

Simple to implement since it only requires an array and an index (top).

More complex, as it requires node creation and pointer manipulation.

Resizing

Requires manual resizing, which involves creating a larger array and copying elements (O(n) complexity).

Grows dynamically without any need for resizing.

Extra Memory Usage

No extra memory is required apart from the array itself.

Requires additional memory for pointers, increasing overhead.

Stack Overflow and Underflow Handling

Stack Overflow occurs when the predefined size is exceeded.

No Stack Overflow, as long as there is available memory.

Application in Recursion

Can cause Stack Overflow in recursive calls if the array limit is reached.

Efficient for recursion, as memory is allocated dynamically.

C program to implement this hospital management system using a linked list-based stack

#include <stdio.h>

#include <stdlib.h>

#include <malloc.h>

#include <string.h>

 

// Structure to store patient details

struct Patient {

    char name[50];

    int age;

    char disease[50];

    struct Patient *next;

};

 

struct Patient *top = NULL;

 

// Function prototypes

struct Patient *push(struct Patient *, char[], int, char[]);

struct Patient *display(struct Patient *);

struct Patient *pop(struct Patient *);

void peek(struct Patient *);

 

int main() {

    int option, age;

    char name[50], disease[50];

 

    do {

        printf("\n *****HOSPITAL PATIENT MANAGEMENT MENU*****");

        printf("\n 1. ADD NEW PATIENT (PUSH)");

        printf("\n 2. DISCHARGE PATIENT (POP)");

        printf("\n 3. SHOW LAST ADMITTED PATIENT (PEEK)");

        printf("\n 4. DISPLAY ALL PATIENTS");

        printf("\n 5. EXIT");

        printf("\n Enter your option: ");

        scanf("%d", &option);

        getchar(); // To consume newline character

 

        switch(option) {

            case 1:

                printf("\n Enter Patient Name: ");

                fgets(name, sizeof(name), stdin);

                name[strcspn(name, "\n")] = 0; // Remove newline

                printf(" Enter Age: ");

                scanf("%d", &age);

                getchar();

                printf(" Enter Disease: ");

                fgets(disease, sizeof(disease), stdin);

                disease[strcspn(disease, "\n")] = 0;

                top = push(top, name, age, disease);

                break;

            case 2:

                top = pop(top);

                break;

            case 3:

                peek(top);

                break;

            case 4:

                top = display(top);

                break;

        }

    } while(option != 5);

    return 0;

}

 

// Function to add a new patient to the stack

struct Patient *push(struct Patient *top, char name[], int age, char disease[]) {

    struct Patient *newPatient;

    newPatient = (struct Patient*)malloc(sizeof(struct Patient));

    strcpy(newPatient->name, name);

    newPatient->age = age;

    strcpy(newPatient->disease, disease);

    newPatient->next = top;

    top = newPatient;

    printf("\n Patient Added: %s, Age: %d, Disease: %s", name, age, disease);

    return top;

}

 

// Function to remove a patient from the stack

struct Patient *pop(struct Patient *top) {

    struct Patient *ptr;

    if(top == NULL) {

        printf("\n NO PATIENTS TO DISCHARGE (STACK UNDERFLOW)");

    } else {

        ptr = top;

        printf("\n Discharging Patient: %s, Age: %d, Disease: %s", ptr->name, ptr->age, ptr->disease);

        top = top->next;

        free(ptr);

    }

    return top;

}

 

// Function to display the last admitted patient (top of the stack)

void peek(struct Patient *top) {

    if(top == NULL) {

        printf("\n NO PATIENTS IN RECORD");

    } else {

        printf("\n Last Admitted Patient: %s, Age: %d, Disease: %s", top->name, top->age, top->disease);

    }

}

 

// Function to display all patients

struct Patient *display(struct Patient *top) {

    struct Patient *ptr;

    ptr = top;

    if(top == NULL) {

        printf("\n NO PATIENTS IN RECORD");

    } else {

        printf("\n\n LIST OF PATIENTS: ");

        while(ptr != NULL) {

            printf("\n %s, Age: %d, Disease: %s", ptr->name, ptr->age, ptr->disease);

            ptr = ptr->next;

        }

    }

    return top;

}

 

 how this approach is better than an array-based stack for this scenario:

A linked list-based stack is the best choice for a hospital patient record system because:

✔ No size limitations

✔ Efficient memory usage

✔ Faster insertions & deletions

✔ Memory is freed when a patient is discharged

✔ Can handle an unpredictable number of patients

 

Using an array-based stack would restrict the number of patients and lead to memory inefficiencies. Hence, a linked list-based stack provides better flexibility and efficiency for this scenario.
